title: These are the House races to watch in the 2026 midterm election on Nov. 3
description: A worker holds I Voted Today stickers du
body:
A worker holds I Voted Today stickers during early voting on October 14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa.
                
                    Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images
    

   
   In the final week of the 2026 midterm election, ad spending data suggests the core battle is less about stopping a Democratic wave in the House, and more about figuring out how high it crests.   An NPR analysis finds the final competitive House landscape is expansive, including 70 districts where both parties are investing at least six figures per district into their final days of messaging.    Loading... 
   That includes more than $10 million each in toss up districts in Michigan, North Carolina, New York and Florida; seven figure ad buys in deep-red communities across Tennessee, Oklahoma and Arkansas and last-minute resources to districts where gerrymandering by Republicans could backfire.   
   In a midterm environment that disfavors the party in power, Republicans' narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House appears all but certain to give way to Democratic control. The latest ratings from the Cook Political Report finds Democrats favored in 220 seats, 17 listed as "toss-ups" and another 30 that are potentially competitive but lean toward the GOP.   
   Competitive races on paper   Most of the seats that saw narrow margins in the 2024 presidential election cycle have shifted the way of the Democrats, especially in the 10 districts that voted for one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House nominee.   That includes seats held by Democratic Reps. Adam Gray (CA-13), Nellie Pou (NJ-09) and Marie Gluesenkamp-Perez (WA-03) and retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon (NE-02).   All four of those districts have seen Republicans slash ad reservations in recent weeks, according to AdImpact data.   The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds Democrats have a 10-point advantage among registered voters and 8 points with likely voters on the generic congressional ballot. That means a far broader number of seats are competitive on paper, before accounting for candidate quality or outside spending.   Cost of living remains the top concern for voters, as rising gas prices, tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran factor into economic woes for many Americans. At the same time, a record number of Congressional retirement announcements has been amplified by an anti-incumbency streak in primary elections.   
   A wave of mid-decade redistricting after a Supreme Court decision that further rolled back part of the Voting Rights Act further scrambled the map, as Republicans shifted boundary lines to add more conservative voters into districts held by Democratic Reps. Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), Don Davis (NC-01), Shomari Figures (AL-02) and Darren Soto (FL-09).   (Democrats did the same in California for the districts currently held by Republican Reps. James Gallagher (CA-01), David Valadao (CA-22), Ken Calvert (CA-41), Darrell Issa (CA-48) and independent Kevin Kiley (CA-06)).   Only Figures and Soto are in districts that are rated as currently favoring Republicans.   
   Big spending in many places   
   As millions of voters have already cast their ballots in the midterms, there are dozens of races Democrats and Republicans consider worthy of heavy investment in the final hours to help shape the outcome.   Most expensive among them: Michigan's 7th District and North Carolina's 1st District —each with more than $12 million in spending planned; Florida's 14th, 22nd and 25th Districts; New York's 17th District; Iowa's 2nd and 3rd Districts and a slew of other races that either favor Democrats or are considered toss ups.   They include seats redrawn by Republicans this year to minimize Democratic voting power, like Alabama's 2nd District and Tennessee's 9th District and districts where voters backed Trump in 2024 by more than 10 points like Kentucky's 6th District and Arkansas' 2nd District.   In all, the 70 races that have at least six figures of ad spending from each party voted for Trump by an average of 9 points in 2024.   There are 60 districts that are listed as priorities of both the Democratic and Republican House campaign arms, highlighting the impact of the Trump administration's unpopularity with voters over the last year.   Not every race will end up close or see party control change hands. Many of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "Districts In Play," for example, gave Trump closer to 60% of the vote in 2024 and have seen little-to-no ad spend from either party.

title: Alaska's all-important Senate race is roiled by a report on alleged spoiler candidate
description: This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Su
body:
This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, left, and another Senate candidate named Dan Sullivan.
                
                    Mark Thiessen, Becky Bohrer/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Thiessen, Becky Bohrer/AP
    

   
   Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation after a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.   That story detailed efforts by Democratic campaign operatives to recruit what Republicans have long alleged is a spoiler candidate whose presence on the ballot could confuse voters and siphon support from the GOP incumbent. The two candidates share the name Dan Sullivan.   NPR hasn't independently confirmed the Times' reporting, but it's roiled the Senate race just days before Election Day. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, is hoping to flip the seat for her party.   
   The Times' story is based on interviews and communications among Peltola's attorneys and advisers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.   Democrats have long denied involvement in the non-incumbent Sullivan's candidacy, and both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC reiterated those denials after the Times story published.   While campaigning Wednesday, Peltola called the story a distraction, according to Alaska Public Media, and the non-incumbent Sullivan did not respond to Alaska Public Media's requests for comment. He has previously said it was his decision to run for Senate.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mary Peltola, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, addresses supporters at an election watch party on Aug. 18 in Anchorage.
                
                    Mark Thiessen/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Thiessen/AP
    

   
   Republicans have pounced on the news.   "Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan, said in a statement. President Trump called it "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level," in an online post.   Trump's Justice Department had already sought to intervene in the Senate race, asking a court last week to delay certification if the incumbent Sullivan loses by a small margin. The legal effort cited potential voter confusion stemming from the second Sullivan on the ballot.   Election law experts had broadly criticized the DOJ's case as weak, in part because the Constitution grants states control over elections.   
   The Sullivan candidacies had already been probed by state officials, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the non-incumbent Sullivan could appear on the general election ballot.   Justice Department officials said Thursday the Times' story expands its options for investigating the Senate race, and it filed an amended complaint citing the new reporting.   And in the wake of the Times story, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said Wednesday night that he is directing the state's Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."   It's unclear what laws could have been violated.   Trickery has been fairly common in politics, and it can be difficult to write laws that prevent shenanigans, according to Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who's co-authored a book on dirty tricks in campaigns.   "There's just a lot of tricks," Kamarck told NPR. "There's old ones. There's new ones. In this day and age, the internet makes it really easy to get the word out, both on a trick or, frankly, on a correction to a trick. But it's pretty standard fare for campaigns."   At times major-party advisers will seek to boost third-party candidates, in an effort to undercut the other major-party's candidate. Some voters who spoke with Alaska Public Media compared the new reporting about the Sullivan case to Republican groups' spending in support of a Democrat who's a federal prisoner in New York but who's on Alaska's U.S. House ballot.   
   The second, non-incumbent Sullivan advanced to the general election after Alaska's nonpartisan primary that sends the top four vote-getters to the fall ballot.   Alaska Public Media found mixed reactions to the Times' reporting, with some residents frustrated that it's drawing attention from other issues, and others expressing skepticism that voters would be confused. The ballot notes which Sullivan is the Republican incumbent.   Some experts have pointed out that all the news about the second Sullivan's candidacy could reduce any voter confusion. And because the state has a ranked-choice voting system for the general election, if voters are confused, they could rank both Sullivans and not rank Peltola.   
   Whether voters want to keep the state's unique election system is also on the general election ballot.   NPR's Hansi Lo Wang and Ryan Lucas contributed reporting.

title: Hackers expose the identities of more than 40,000 DHS employees
description: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security
body:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security emblem on the U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement building as seen on January 07, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America
    

   
   A hacking group cracked the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of more than 40,000 DHS agents, operatives, and associates, on Wednesday, including those involved in undercover operations.   "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," a spokesperson for the hacktivist group behind the breach, the Department of Peace, said in an online statement.   The hackers said they stole the data by subverting DHS's single sign on system, according to an online post. It said it distributed that material to the group Distributed Denial of Secrets, which posted it online in a database called Icepick. The Department of Peace also shared the trove of data with Ryan Ottignon, a U.S.-based journalist, and a Swiss activist known as maia arson crimew. Together, the two created a searchable online database, with crimew doing all of the technical work, Ottignon told NPR.   
   DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity," because it makes explicit connections between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations …along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."   Other activists say the information will be a boon to those investigating DHS and filing freedom of information requests, which, due to a lack of specific information, like names, email addresses, can often yield useless results.   In a statement, DHS said it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The department added that it is taking necessary steps to "ensure all are properly protected."   More than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Another 10,000 relate to Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and its Homeland Security Investigations unit.   It is an unprecedented breach of intelligence, coming on the heels of similar hacking attacks at the FBI. However, the database is far from comprehensive and represents about a fifth of Homeland Security's workforce, which staffs a little more than 220,000 people.   Ottignon, who has worked on similar data leak projects in the past, rejected suggestions that he and others connected to the Department of Peace or Distribution Denials of Secrets were doxing government employees.   
   "We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around into cities and states and all around the country, and they seek to hide who they are. Very frequently using masks, wearing plain clothes. And they do universally unspeakable things to these communities," Ottignon said. He added that he believed that kind of behavior is unacceptable in a free society.   "We need oversight for useful government, if it exists at all. So this is just one step in that oversight process," he added.   In a note attached to the files, the Department of Peace wrote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs."

title: Support for Trump among white evangelicals has plummeted, polls reveal
description: Support for Trump among white evangelicals has plummeted, polls reveal   Three new polls suggest that President Trump is losing ground among white eva
body:
Support for Trump among white evangelicals has plummeted, polls reveal   Three new polls suggest that President Trump is losing ground among white evangelicals. What explains this drop — and will it affect the midterm elections?

    
        Politics
    


      
                  
            October 29, 20264:44 AM ET
         
      
   
                              By                
            


      
      Support for Trump among white evangelicals has plummeted, polls reveal
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6012410/nx-s1-9983203" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      Three new polls suggest that President Trump is losing ground among white evangelicals. What explains this drop — and will it affect the midterm elections?   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  White evangelicals are usually President Trump's most loyal backers. New polling shows their support for Trump has plummeted. Jack Jenkins of Religion News Service talked to evangelicals about what's behind the shift.JACK JENKINS, BYLINE: Pastor Robert Jeffress is best known for two things - serving as pastor of First Baptist Church in Dallas, Texas, and being one of the most vocal evangelical supporters of President Trump. But while Jeffress remains bullish on Trump, he's concerned about how factors like prices at the pump are pulling the president's approval rating down.ROBERT JEFFRESS: You know, evangelicals have to fill up their tanks with gasoline as well.KRISTIN DU MEZ: Yeah. This is probably one of the very few times I'll go on record agreeing with Robert Jeffress.JENKINS: That's Kristin Du Mez, a historian who studies evangelicalism at Calvin University.DU MEZ: Inasmuch as there is a decline in evangelical support for Trump, I would interpret it in terms of the economy, in terms of, you know, these general trends that we're seeing across nearly every demographic.JENKINS: Since 2016, white evangelicals have formed the most loyal part of Trump's base. Around 8 in 10 approved of his actions in the White House as of early last year. But the number has been dropping precipitously in recent weeks. Now three polls all show double-digit declines in his support among white evangelicals. According to a Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month, Trump's approval rating has dropped 20 points from 78% to 58%.RALPH REED: We're hearing what you would expect to hear, which is concerns about cost of living, concerns about gas prices.JENKINS: That's Ralph Reed, a longtime evangelical activist and political consultant known as one of the architects of the religious right. And there may be other factors beyond dollars and cents here. Michael Weir is a Democrat and an evangelical organizer who helped former President Obama court religious voters. He says Trump's drop in support among conservative Christians may signal a bit of evangelical exhaustion with the president.MICHAEL WEIR: I don't think we're going to see massive, massive swings of conservative evangelicals voting for Democrats, but there is a bit of buyer's remorse, a bit of this is not what we signed up for, a bit of just weariness with it all.JENKINS: Du Mez says some evangelicals are trying to rally their faithful back to Trump and Republicans despite the economic woes.DU MEZ: That is rhetoric that I am hearing from conservative evangelicals. Yes, these gas prices are wild right now. But if we are ensuring a safe country for our children, it is all worth it. We are willing to pay the price.JENKINS: The fact that this drop in Trump support has happened on the eve of the congressional midterms makes some conservative activists nervous. Ralph Reed is working hard to combat it. At a Trump rally in Dalton, Georgia, he planned to recruit volunteers to help turn out evangelical voters in the midterm elections. He's peppering evangelical voters with messages that tap into longstanding concerns, namely Democrats' more liberal positions on issues such as Israel, LGBTQ rights and abortion.REED: You get into the pro-life issues and the gender issues. And all that is on our voter guides that are going into churches. It's on all the door hangers.JENKINS: In the past, Trump's support among evangelicals has dipped and then recovered. But it has never dropped this far, this close to an election. And now the key question is whether this downward trend will continue.For NPR News, I'm Jack Jenkins.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: State ballots let voters decide on abortion, taxes, transgender restrictions
description: A scene from early voting in Maryland, w
body:
A scene from early voting in Maryland, where voters can decide whether to allow congressional redistricting. It's one of more than 140 state ballot questions around the country this election.
                
                    Allison Robbert/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Allison Robbert/AP
    

   
   Whether or not they live in a competitive congressional district, voters in many states will be deciding on statewide ballot measures with a chance to make law themselves.   There are 145 statewide ballot measures on the November ballot, according to Ballotpedia, which tracks elections.   In some cases the questions were put on the ballot with petition drives by citizens frustrated with the actions - or lack of action - by their state lawmakers. In many cases, legislatures go to the voters with amendments to their state constitution.   There are common themes across the country: many of the most high profile referenda are on abortion, LGBTQ+ rights, taxes, and voting.   
   Four years after Dobbs, states are still going back and forth on abortion   Four states have abortion on the ballot. That comes after a flurry of ballot measures on the issue since federal protections for the procedure from Roe v. Wade were overturned by the Dobbs decision in 2022.   
   Just two years ago, Missouri voters nullified what had been one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. But the Republican-led legislature has put the question back on the ballot. And lawmakers crafted a single question that includes both a near-total ban on abortion and prohibitions on gender-affirming medical treatments for minors.   Much of the advertising for the measure just mentions the gender-affirming care ban, which would go into the state constitution to strengthen bans already in state law.   Abortion is legal in Nevada and Virginia but voters in both states will have a chance to put those rights in the state constitution. That would make it harder for future legislatures to ban abortion.   A vote in Idaho could overturn that state's near-total ban on abortion.   States consider transgender restrictions or guaranteeing LGBTQ+ rights    Rights for LGBTQ+ people have been hotly contested in the states in recent years. Several states have them on the ballot.   
   In Vermont a proposal would amend the state constitution to include an equal protection clause that would guarantee rights for gender identity and gender expression.   Virginia voters could strengthen laws allowing same-sex marriage. The state currently has an old ban on same-sex marriage in its constitution - although it is not in force due to a 2015 US Supreme Court decision. Voters are deciding whether to replace that language through an amendment that would define marriage as between any two adults regardless of race, sex, or gender.   Arizona and Colorado have proposals to ban transgender students in girls school and college sports, with Arizona expanding a current ban by including restrictions on locker rooms and other areas.   A proposal in Washington state would require that a student wanting to play girls sports have their biological sex confirmed by their healthcare provider based on, "the student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In California, Prop. 40 asks voters to impose a wealth tax on billionaires to pay for healthcare programs and two other propositions would block the tax. Opponents say it would chase billionaires out of the state, costing the state money in the long run.
                
                    Jae C. Hong/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jae C. Hong/AP
    

   
   A billionaire tax highlights fiscal measures   Taxes and state finances make up the largest category of ballot measures.   The highest-profile proposition is in California, where voters could impose a novel kind of billionaire tax. Prop. 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires, including their ownership in companies.   Proponents say the Republican Congress gave tax breaks to billionaires by cutting health care programs so it's fair to tax them to make up the cuts. Opponents, including some prominent Democrats, say it will just chase billionaires to other states. Two competing measures on the same ballot would block the tax.   A coalition of progressive Coloradans is backing a proposal that could result in higher income taxes for those making over $500,000 a year.   States are also putting limits on taxation before voters: Tennessee's legislature sent voters a proposal to ban state-mandated property taxes. Iowa's General Assembly is asking voters to approve a constitutional amendment requiring certain tax law changes to go to require two-thirds of both of the legislature's chambers to pass.   
   Florida lawmakers put a question on the ballot that would exempt the first $150,000 of a home's value from property taxes, having huge implications for the local governments that depend on that funding.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Activists rally in support of a proposed constitutional amendment near the state capitol in Jefferson City in August.
                
                    David A. Lieb/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        David A. Lieb/AP
    

   
   Many states are voting about voting   In some states, voters are facing questions that could make it harder for them to change the law through their votes in the future.   Proposals in North Dakota and South Dakota would require future amendments to the state constitution to have 60% voter approval instead of a simple majority. Utah has a similar question for tax proposals.   In Missouri, voters could go the other way – making it harder for lawmakers to overturn future voter initiatives. And they face another question about whether to allow congressional redistricting that could help Republicans flip a House seat held by a Democrat in 2028.   In Maryland, voters can approve a congressional redistricting that would likely favor Democrats.   There are several other voting issues on ballots in other states.   Coloradans are considering a proposal to require ballot questions to be written in plain, 8th grade level English.   Montanans could approve a state-level work around of the Citizens United Supreme Court decision that has led to an explosion of hard-to-track money in campaigns. The measure would do that by redefining corporations so they can't give unlimited political donations. But that could be blocked by the courts.   Several states, including California, Nevada and North Carolina have proposals to require photo ID when voting.   And in Virginia, voters will decide if some people are entitled to the right to vote at all: people convicted of felonies need to have their rights restored by the governor.      Jahd Khalil covers Virginia State Politics for VPM.

schema.headline: State ballots let voters decide on abortion, taxes, transgender restrictions

title: Fishing is a key issue in Alaska's tight U.S. Senate race
description: Alaska's U.S. Senate race is embroiled in an emotional fight over fish. Many in the state rely upon salmon to feed their families but those fis
body:
Alaska's U.S. Senate race is embroiled in an emotional fight over fish. Many in the state rely upon salmon to feed their families but those fish and others are increasingly hard to find.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:  President Trump is trying to preemptively block election results in Alaska if the Republican incumbent loses. But in that state, the big issue in the Senate race has been an emotional fight over fish. And that's because the salmon that have long sustained Indigenous people are not returning to some Western Alaska rivers. While people living in remote villages feel the loss of salmon most acutely, the issue could ultimately affect the balance of power thousands of miles away in Washington, D.C. Alaska public media's Liz Ruskin reports.(SOUNDBITE OF DOG BARKING)LIZ RUSKIN, BYLINE: Evon Waska lives at the water's edge, where he says his parents settled when they gave up their nomadic life.EVON WASKA: Well, this is my smokehouse, and this is where we make smoke, right?RUSKIN: Waska's drying racks should be filled with salmon, but they're empty. Most years now, too few salmon return from the Bering Sea to his river, the Kuskokwim. To conserve fish, government agencies often close the river to fishing, even to those like Waska who fish to feed their families. Waska blames trawlers, industrial fishing boats miles offshore.WASKA: They don't close the trawlers. They close me and my people first.RUSKIN: Waska is up against a $1 billion industry, much of it based in Seattle. Picture a sock-shaped net that's a quarter mile long with an opening as wide as a football field. That's what trawlers tow to catch pollock. The white fish is served to you as imitation crab in McDonald's Filet-O-Fish. But also scooped up in those nets are prized king salmon and other fish. They're caught by accident and wasted, a problem known as bycatch. Alaskans are increasingly angry about it. Now, in a year where Alaska could decide the balance of power in the U.S. Senate, fish are all over political ads here.(SOUNDBITE OF MONTAGE)UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #1: Senator Sullivan is championing legislation to reduce bycatch and strengthen Alaska's fisheries. Call Senator Dan Sullivan. Thank him and tell him to keep fighting for Alaska fishermen.UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: Dan Sullivan is taking big money from out-of-state corporate trawlers.UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #3: Mary Peltola tells a lot of fish tales to get votes.RUSKIN: Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been an ally of the pollock industry. But this year, he's touting a new bill.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)DAN SULLIVAN: It's the most comprehensive bycatch legislation ever to reduce bycatch, protect seafloor habitat.RUSKIN: Democratic Senate challenger Mary Peltola is Indigenous, from the Kuskokwim. She says she'd ban factory trawlers, the largest of the pollock fleet. She calls Sullivan's bill an election year ploy.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARY PELTOLA: Dan Sullivan reeled in over $300,000 from trawlers and waited until the 11th hour for a half-hearted and half-baked solution.RUSKIN: Heather Mann (ph) leads a trawlers association. She says scapegoating the pollock fishery won't help western Alaska.HEATHER MANN: Even if you were to eliminate pollock, the chances of salmon runs being restored, what the science shows us is it would have a minimal impact.RUSKIN: So far this year, pollock trawlers say they've caught 40,000 Alaska salmon. The waste is a tiny percentage of the massive pollock harvest.(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINE WHIRRING)RUSKIN: But in the Kuskokwim River village of Kwethluk, it's galling.(SOUNDBITE OF MACHINE RUMBLING)RUSKIN: Subsistence fishing is the main occupation here and the backbone of the culture. Tribal president Mary Nikolai steps into a neighbor's cold smokehouse. It pains her to see it was unused all summer.MARY NICOLAI: Most of the smokehouses are like this. And it's like a slow trend of closing our workforce out.RUSKIN: Regardless of who wins, she hopes this close Senate race tells the world of the threat they face.For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Kwethluk, Alaska.

title: GDP report to give insight before Election Day. And, Israel's election is deadlocked
description: Midterm Spending Blitz, GDP & Inflations Reports, Israel Election Deadlock & Iran War
body:
Midterm Spending Blitz, GDP & Inflations Reports, Israel Election Deadlock & Iran War
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-150614/nx-s1-mx-6021969-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   As Election Day approaches, data suggest that the focus is now less on whether a Democratic wave will happen and more on its potential magnitude. Democrats continue to invest in competitive Republican-dominated races, and Republicans are matching those efforts. An NPR analysis found 70 districts where both Democrats and Republicans are investing more than six figures in their final messaging. These are the races to watch.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A worker holds I Voted Today stickers during early voting on October 14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa.
                
                    Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Former President Barack Obama campaigned last night in Georgia for Democrats, highlighting the high cost of living and how Trump's policies contribute to rising prices, NPR's Stephen Fowler tells Up First. Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is likely to win the Senate race, while Georgia's governor race remains uncertain. Millions have already cast their votes early, and Fowler says data show increased turnout among Latino and young voters in Democratic areas, as well as among non-supervoters, who typically don't participate in primaries. The trend creates some uncertainty around what the final electorate will look like, and indicates that Republicans will have to rely on a large Election Day turnout to stay competitive, Fowler says.➡️ A federal judge has denied the Department of Justice's emergency request to halt the processing of ballots for 20,000 individuals it identified as "likely" noncitizens. The department filed a notice that it is appealing the decision.➡️ Across the U.S., voters will see 145 statewide ballot measures on the November ballot, according to Ballotpedia. Key themes include abortion, LGBTQ+ rights, taxes, and voting.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   
   Americans will receive a final reading on the country's gross domestic product and the state of inflation today before next week's midterm election. The report will show whether the economy grew faster in the summer compared to spring. Economists expect GDP to be higher, but some say the growth feels delicate.   🎧 The tech industry's continued investment in artificial intelligence and consumer spending are driving the GDP, NPR's Stephan Bisaha says. But economist Mark Zandi tells him it's a "very, very fragile growth." Zandi blames inflation for this sense of fragility. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, and prices are outpacing wage growth. After keeping interest rates steady yesterday, the Fed will be paying close attention to today's inflation reading from the Commerce Department.   Israel's election is in a deadlock. More than 90% of the votes have been counted, and no candidate has a clear path to forming a coalition. Parties need 61 seats in parliament for a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have secured 53 seats, while his top rival Gadi Eisenkot and his allies have garnered 48.   🎧 NPR's Daniel Estrin says there are several options for breaking the impasse. Eisenkot's camp could win by partnering with Arab-led parties, which recently secured a record 19 seats in parliament, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. But this partnership seems unlikely due to the political risks. Estrin says Arab political leaders in Israel have been demonized. Israel could hold repeat elections, but Eisenkot doesn't want that because the opposition would have a hard time getting votes a second time. Estrin says Eisenkot will be under pressure to enter a unity government with Netanyahu, especially if Israel launches a new war with Iran.   
   A lawsuit filed yesterday against the Department of Education alleges that the Trump administration is illegally refusing to follow the rules of a program known as "closed school discharge." For more than three decades, federal law has required the U.S. Secretary of Education to cancel debts for qualified borrowers when their schools close unexpectedly. Student Defense, a nonprofit borrower advocacy group, filed the suit on behalf of potentially thousands of borrowers. The Education Department told NPR it stands by its implementation of the program.   Today's listen   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Bernie Taupin speaks onstage during the Keynote Conversation: Bernie Taupin and Brandi Carlile during AMERICANAFEST 2026 at The Embassy Suites Nashville on Sept. 16, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee.
                
                    Erika Goldring/Getty Images for Americana Music
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Erika Goldring/Getty Images for Americana Music
    

   
   Bernie Taupin is Elton John's lyricist on nearly every album. Now, for the first time in 40 years, he's stepping into the spotlight. His new album, The Sea Has No Mercy, features a collection of songs entirely written and sung by him. Taupin admits that until recently, he hadn't considered writing for himself, but now he's ready to share his own musical voice. He tells Morning Edition's A Martínez that more so than a songwriter and a lyricist, Taupin thinks of himself as a storyteller. Listen to snippets of the album and hear about how Taupin has been able to keep his and John's relationship so strong.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Medicare chief Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks at an event announcing the artificial intelligence website, America.gov  in Washington, D.C., last month.
                
                    Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Medicare's open enrollment window runs through Dec. 7. More than half of Americans in Medicare choose a Medicare Advantage plan, which is run by private insurers instead of the federal government. Medicare Advantage is popular because it covers dental and vision, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. But private carriers can pick and choose where it's offered, and withdraw from unprofitable communities. Over the last three years, insurers have left regions on an increasingly large scale, according to recent JAMA research. Here are some tips to help navigate Medicare open enrollment this year:   ➡️ Check if your Medicare Advantage plan is still offered. Plans closing should have sent letters in early October. You can also log in to Medicare.gov to verify your plan's status.➡️ Try calling your state's State Health Insurance Assistance Program. It's free, federally mandated and offers unbiased information on all options. Visit shiphelp.org to find your state's program.➡️ Look for local Medicare counseling services. Brokers can be helpful, but make sure to choose one who discusses all your options, including traditional Medicare and supplemental plans.➡️ Double-check anything you see on Medicare's Plan Finder with your doctor's office or other Medicare assister.➡️ Be cautious about sharing your personal information, such as your phone number. Some online agencies may sell it, leading to spam calls and potential scams.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                COLMA, CALIFORNIA - JANUARY 06:  Ford pickup trucks are displayed on the sales lot at Serramonte Ford on January 06, 2026 in Colma, California.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
    

   
   American automakers reported increased revenues for the third quarter but face serious challenges. They are paying more for key components like computer chips, steel and copper, as well as higher transport fuel costs.A hacking group breached the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files yesterday, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of over 40,000 DHS agents and associates, including those in undercover operations.The Department of Health and Human Services announced a new policy that will let small compounding pharmacies make six peptides that haven't been approved by the Food and Drug Administration. title: Judge denies the Justice Department's bid to stop processing California ballots
description: People extract ballots from their envelo
body:
People extract ballots from their envelopes and prepare them to be scanned for counting in the Vote-By-Mail Processing Boards area at the Orange County Registrar of Voters Facility in Santa Ana, Calif., on Oct. 28.
                
                    Apu Gomes/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Apu Gomes/Getty Images
    

   
   A federal judge has denied an unprecedented, emergency request by the Department of Justice to segregate thousands of California ballots in the midterm elections.   The Justice Department wants California election officials to stop processing ballots pertaining to 20,000 individuals that federal officials say are "likely" noncitizens.   
   State and local officials in California have countered that the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is unreliable, with a preliminary analysis by Los Angeles County showing that many on the list do not have active voter registrations. The officials also claim that setting aside ballots just days before Election Day, when voting and processing mailed ballots are already underway, would be unlawful and infeasible and would disenfranchise eligible voters.   In his 26-page ruling issued Wednesday evening, U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, denied the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order to stop processing the ballots in question.   
   "Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," he wrote.   Carter also expressed concern about taking action that could disenfranchise eligible voters and create chaos.   "Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote at the conclusion of his order. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process."   
   The judge said that the federal government can address the issue by continuing to indict people for the crime of illegally voting as noncitizens. DOJ officials say in the last two months they have charged dozens of people for registering or voting without being a U.S. citizen.   The DOJ's lawsuit in California, which was filed Oct. 15, is among a flurry of unprecedented actions the department has waged in states close to Election Day, raising alarms about federal interference in state election procedures.   Like in California, on Monday federal prosecutors asked Washington state election officials to review a list of 400 registered voters the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens. And last week, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit in Alaska that seeks to stop the state from certifying the results in its Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses due to votes for a longshot candidate with a similar name who is accused of being a spoiler candidate.   
   In California's most recent motion to the court, state Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, asked the judge to take into account the circumstances of DOJ's demand. "This litigation is a precursor to further interference here in California," Bonta wrote. "The Court must not be drawn into this chilling degradation of democratic values and constitutional principles."   The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice that it is appealing Carter's denial. The matter could ultimately wind up before the U.S. Supreme Court.   "Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution," Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, wrote on X, adding that he would be seeking an emergency order from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.    The DOJ has argued the issue is urgent since once signatures are verified on returned mail ballot envelopes, the ballots are separated from their envelopes to retain voter confidentiality, making it impossible to retrieve an ineligible ballot.    Voting by noncitizens has been shown by audits and investigations to be extremely rare.   "Tonight's decision makes clear that the federal government's actions are election interference," said Jonathan Miller, chief program officer at Public Rights Project, which is counsel for Los Angeles County.   "The district court unequivocally found that DOJ's claims are unsubstantiated, that it has no basis to bring its lawsuit, and it has presented no evidence to justify its actions. The administration claims to be protecting election integrity while, at every turn, undermining the systems and federal support that safeguard our elections," Miller said.   Bonta, California's attorney general, said in a statement the ruling is an important victory, "But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California's elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed."   The accuracy of the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is still an ongoing matter of dispute.   
   A Los Angeles County analysis of a small sample of people on the DOJ's list found that a significant portion had said in records they were born in the U.S. But U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services senior official Nicolas Bartell contested that in recent court filings, writing that his office's review of those individuals found none were U.S.-born.   Bartell did acknowledge the review found four of those people "might have a claim to U.S. citizenship."   He also provided the court additional details about the federal government's methodology in creating the list in recent court filings.   But University of Delaware political scientist Kassra Oskooi, who has been tapped as an expert witness by voting rights groups who are intervening in the case, responded in his own declaration to the court that he believes USCIS's matching protocol "is likely to be unreliable."   Carter wrote in his order the federal government's protocol "raises significant concerns" and that he could not conclude its process is credible.
